tutorials.title: OpenAPI/Swagger: Complete Guide
tutorials.description: OpenAPI 3.0.x specification, YAML/JSON structure, paths, operations, parameters, responses, schemas, security schemes, and Swagger UI/Editor.

content.value:
OpenAPI, formerly known as Swagger, is the industry-standard specification for describing REST APIs. It provides a language-agnostic way to define your API's structure, including endpoints, request parameters, response formats, authentication methods, and more. Think of it as a blueprint for your API—a single source of truth that both humans and machines can understand.

With an OpenAPI definition, you can automatically generate documentation, create client SDKs in dozens of languages, validate requests and responses, and build mock servers—all from one file. This makes it an essential tool for API design-first development and team collaboration.

content.title: OpenAPI vs Swagger: The Name Story
content.explanation:
The terminology can be confusing. Here's the simple breakdown:

- **Swagger** was the original name of the specification created by Reverb (formerly Wordnik) in 2011.
- In 2015, the specification was donated to the OpenAPI Initiative under the Linux Foundation and renamed **OpenAPI**.
- **Swagger** now refers to the tooling ecosystem (Swagger UI, Swagger Editor, Swagger Codegen) built around the OpenAPI specification.

So when someone says "Swagger file," they usually mean an OpenAPI specification file. When they say "Swagger UI," they mean the documentation tool.

content.value: An OpenAPI document is a JSON or YAML file that follows a specific structure. Here's the high-level anatomy of an OpenAPI 3.0 document:

content.caption: Basic OpenAPI Structure
content.code:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Sample API
  description: A sample API to demonstrate OpenAPI
  version: 1.0.0
servers:
  - url: https://api.example.com/v1
paths:
  /users:
    get:
      summary: Returns a list of users
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK
components:
  schemas:
    User:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
        name:
          type: string
security:
  - apiKey: []
tags:
  - name: users
    description: User operations

content.value: The info object provides metadata about your API. It's required and appears at the top of your OpenAPI document.

content.caption: Info Object Example
content.code:
info:
  title: User Management API
  description: |
    A comprehensive API for managing users in your application.
    Supports CRUD operations, authentication, and user preferences.
  version: 2.1.0
  termsOfService: https://example.com/terms
  contact:
    name: API Support
    email: support@example.com
    url: https://example.com/support
  license:
    name: Apache 2.0
    url: https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html

content.value: The servers object specifies one or more base URLs for your API. This is where clients will send requests.

content.caption: Servers with Multiple Environments
content.code:
servers:
  - url: https://api.example.com/v1
    description: Production server
  - url: https://staging-api.example.com/v1
    description: Staging server
  - url: http://localhost:3000/api/v1
    description: Local development

content.caption: Servers with Variables
content.code:
servers:
  - url: https://{environment}.example.com/{basePath}
    description: Dynamic server selection
    variables:
      environment:
        enum:
          - api
          - staging-api
          - dev-api
        default: api
      basePath:
        default: v1
        description: API version

content.value: The paths object is the heart of your OpenAPI document. It defines all the endpoints your API exposes and the operations available on each endpoint.

content.caption: Basic Path Structure
content.code:
paths:
  /users:
    get:
      summary: Get all users
      description: Returns a paginated list of users
      tags: [users]
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Successful response
    post:
      summary: Create a user
      description: Creates a new user
      tags: [users]
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/UserCreate'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: User created
  /users/{userId}:
    get:
      summary: Get user by ID
      parameters:
        - name: userId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: integer
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK
        '404':
          description: User not found

content.value: Each path can have one or more operations (HTTP methods). Here's what goes into an operation definition.

content.caption: Complete GET Operation
content.code:
get:
  summary: Get all users
  description: Returns a paginated list of users with optional filtering
  operationId: getUsers
  tags:
    - users
  parameters:
    - name: page
      in: query
      schema:
        type: integer
        minimum: 1
        default: 1
      description: Page number
    - name: limit
      in: query
      schema:
        type: integer
        minimum: 1
        maximum: 100
        default: 20
      description: Items per page
    - name: role
      in: query
      schema:
        type: string
        enum: [admin, user, guest]
      description: Filter by user role
  responses:
    '200':
      description: Successful response
      content:
        application/json:
          schema:
            type: object
            properties:
              data:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'
              total:
                type: integer
              page:
                type: integer
              pages:
                type: integer
    '400':
      description: Invalid parameters
      content:
        application/json:
          schema:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
    '500':
      description: Server error
  security:
    - apiKey: []

content.value: Parameters define inputs to your API operations. They can come from different locations: path, query, header, or cookie.

content.caption: Parameter Examples
content.code:
parameters:
  # Path parameter
  - name: userId
    in: path
    required: true
    schema:
      type: integer
      minimum: 1
    description: The user's unique ID

  # Query parameter
  - name: search
    in: query
    schema:
      type: string
      maxLength: 100
    description: Search term for filtering users

  # Header parameter
  - name: X-Request-ID
    in: header
    schema:
      type: string
      format: uuid
    description: Client request ID for tracing

  # Cookie parameter
  - name: sessionId
    in: cookie
    schema:
      type: string
    description: Session identifier

content.value: The request body describes what data the client should send, typically for POST, PUT, and PATCH operations.

content.caption: Request Body with Multiple Content Types
content.code:
requestBody:
  required: true
  content:
    application/json:
      schema:
        $ref: '#/components/schemas/UserCreate'
      example:
        name: John Doe
        email: john@example.com
        password: secret123
        role: user
    application/x-www-form-urlencoded:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          name:
            type: string
          email:
            type: string
            format: email
          password:
            type: string
            format: password
    multipart/form-data:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          file:
            type: string
            format: binary
            description: User avatar image

content.value: Responses define what your API returns. You should document every possible HTTP status code your API might return.

content.caption: Complete Response Definitions
content.code:
responses:
  '200':
    description: Successful operation
    headers:
      X-RateLimit-Limit:
        schema:
          type: integer
        description: Request limit per hour
      X-RateLimit-Remaining:
        schema:
          type: integer
        description: Remaining requests
    content:
      application/json:
        schema:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'
        examples:
          basic:
            summary: Basic user info
            value:
              id: 1
              name: John Doe
          detailed:
            summary: Detailed user with preferences
            value:
              id: 1
              name: John Doe
              email: john@example.com
              preferences:
                newsletter: true
                theme: dark
  '400':
    description: Bad request
    content:
      application/json:
        schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            code:
              type: string
            message:
              type: string
            details:
              type: array
              items:
                type: object
        examples:
          validation-error:
            value:
              code: VALIDATION_ERROR
              message: Invalid input data
              details:
                - field: email
                  error: must be a valid email
  '404':
    description: Resource not found
    content:
      application/json:
        schema:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/NotFoundError'
  '500':
    description: Internal server error
    content:
      application/json:
        schema:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/ServerError'

content.value: Schemas define the structure of your data. They're defined in the components section and can be reused throughout your document.

content.caption: Schema Examples
content.code:
components:
  schemas:
    User:
      type: object
      required:
        - id
        - name
        - email
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
          readOnly: true
          description: Auto-generated ID
        name:
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 100
          description: User's full name
        email:
          type: string
          format: email
          description: User's email address
        age:
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          maximum: 150
          description: User's age in years
        role:
          type: string
          enum: [admin, user, guest]
          default: user
          description: User's role for authorization
        createdAt:
          type: string
          format: date-time
          readOnly: true
          description: When the user was created
        address:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/Address'
    
    Address:
      type: object
      properties:
        street:
          type: string
        city:
          type: string
        state:
          type: string
          maxLength: 2
        zipCode:
          type: string
          pattern: '^\d{5}(-\d{4})?$'
        country:
          type: string
          default: USA
    
    UserCreate:
      type: object
      required:
        - name
        - email
        - password
      properties:
        name:
          type: string
          minLength: 1
        email:
          type: string
          format: email
        password:
          type: string
          format: password
          minLength: 8
        role:
          type: string
          enum: [user, admin]
          default: user
    
    Error:
      type: object
      properties:
        code:
          type: string
        message:
          type: string
        requestId:
          type: string
          format: uuid
        timestamp:
          type: string
          format: date-time

content.value: Security schemes define how clients authenticate with your API. OpenAPI supports multiple authentication methods.

content.caption: Security Schemes Examples
content.code:
components:
  securitySchemes:
    # API Key in header
    apiKey:
      type: apiKey
      in: header
      name: X-API-Key
      description: API key authentication
    
    # HTTP Basic Auth
    basicAuth:
      type: http
      scheme: basic
      description: Basic HTTP authentication
    
    # Bearer token (JWT)
    bearerAuth:
      type: http
      scheme: bearer
      bearerFormat: JWT
      description: JWT bearer token
    
    # OAuth2 with authorization code flow
    oauth2:
      type: oauth2
      flows:
        authorizationCode:
          authorizationUrl: https://example.com/oauth/authorize
          tokenUrl: https://example.com/oauth/token
          refreshUrl: https://example.com/oauth/refresh
          scopes:
            read: Read user data
            write: Modify user data
            admin: Admin operations
    
    # OpenID Connect
    openId:
      type: openIdConnect
      openIdConnectUrl: https://example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration

# Apply globally
security:
  - bearerAuth: []
  - apiKey: []

content.value: The $ref keyword lets you reference components defined elsewhere, keeping your OpenAPI document DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

content.caption: $ref Examples
content.code:
paths:
  /users:
    get:
      parameters:
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/pageParam'
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/limitParam'
      responses:
        '200':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/UserListResponse'
        '400':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/ErrorResponse'

components:
  parameters:
    pageParam:
      name: page
      in: query
      schema:
        type: integer
        default: 1
    limitParam:
      name: limit
      in: query
      schema:
        type: integer
        default: 20
  
  responses:
    UserListResponse:
      description: List of users
      content:
        application/json:
          schema:
            type: array
            items:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'
    ErrorResponse:
      description: Error response
      content:
        application/json:
          schema:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
  
  schemas:
    User:
      $ref: './user-schema.yaml'
    Error:
      $ref: './error-schema.yaml'

content.value: The Swagger ecosystem provides powerful tools to work with OpenAPI definitions.

content.caption: Using Swagger Codegen
content.code:
# Generate Python client
swagger-codegen generate -i openapi.yaml -l python -o client-python

# Generate Node.js server
swagger-codegen generate -i openapi.yaml -l nodejs-server -o server-node

# Generate TypeScript types
typescript-fetch-codegen generate -i openapi.yaml -o typescript-types

content.value: Follow these best practices to create clean, maintainable OpenAPI documents.

content.title: OpenAPI Best Practices
rows: Latest features, better JSON Schema support
Makes docs useful, not just machine-readable

content.caption: CI Validation
content.code:
# Validate OpenAPI in CI
npx swagger-cli validate openapi.yaml

# Or with Python
openapi-spec-validator openapi.yaml

# Linting
speccy lint openapi.yaml

content.value: One of the most powerful uses of OpenAPI is generating tests automatically. Here are common approaches.

content.caption: Generate PyTest from OpenAPI
content.code:
from openapi_core import create_spec
import requests

def test_get_user():
    # Load OpenAPI spec
    with open('openapi.yaml') as f:
        spec = create_spec(yaml.safe_load(f))
    
    # Make request
    response = requests.get('https://api.example.com/users/1')
    
    # Validate against spec
    result = spec.validate_response(
        request={'method': 'GET', 'path': '/users/1'},
        response=response
    )
    assert not result.errors

content.caption: Contract Testing with Dredd
content.code:
# Install dredd
npm install -g dredd

# Run contract tests
dredd openapi.yaml https://api.example.com

# Output:
# pass: GET /users returns 200
# pass: POST /users returns 201
# fail: GET /users/1 returns 404 when user not found

tutorials.title: OpenAPI Validation & Contract Testing
tutorials.description: Validating APIs against OpenAPI specs, automated contract testing, spectral linting, and OpenAPI diff tools for versioning.

content.value:
An OpenAPI specification is more than just documentation—it's a legally binding contract between API providers and consumers. When you publish an OpenAPI spec, you're making a promise: "If you send requests that look like this, I will respond with data that looks like that." Validation is the process of verifying that your API actually keeps that promise.

Think of it like building a house from blueprints. The blueprints (OpenAPI) show where every wall, door, and window goes. Validation is the building inspector who walks through with a tape measure, checking that everything matches the plan. Without validation, you might discover too late that the door is in the wrong place and nothing fits—except in software, that discovery happens when your API consumers start complaining that their applications are broken.

The cost of contract violations is enormous. A single mismatched field can crash mobile apps, corrupt databases, or cause million-dollar trading errors. OpenAPI validation is your insurance policy against these disasters.

content.title: OpenAPI Contract: Promise vs Reality
content: │  │ • Field 'createdAt' wrong format (got date, need datetime)│  │
│  │ RESULT: Every client that expected 'name' will crash      │  │
content.caption: Contract validation ensures API promises match reality

content.value:
The scenario above happens more often than you'd think. A developer renames a field because it "makes more sense," forgetting that dozens of mobile apps, web frontends, and partner integrations rely on the original name. Without validation, this change sails through code review, passes all unit tests, and deploys to production—only to cause a cascade of failures when real traffic hits.

OpenAPI validation prevents this by catching contract violations before they reach production. It's the difference between finding out about a problem when your automated tests run versus when your users start tweeting about your API being broken.

OpenAPI validation isn't a single activity—it's a stack of checks, each catching different kinds of problems at different stages of development. Understanding these layers helps you build a comprehensive validation strategy that catches issues early and often.

content.title: The Validation Pyramid
content.caption: Multiple layers of validation ensure API quality from design to production

content.title: Validation Layers Explained
rows: YAML syntax, OpenAPI schema compliance, reference resolution
Naming conventions, documentation completeness, best practices
Individual API calls match schema at runtime
All documented endpoints work as specified
Changes between versions that break clients

content.value: Before you do anything else, you must ensure your OpenAPI file itself is valid. An invalid spec is worse than no spec—it gives false confidence and will cause every tool that reads it to fail. This is the foundation upon which everything else is built.

content.title: Spec Validation Process
content: │  │  │ Tries to parse the file as YAML                      │ │  │ │
│  │  │ ❌ Error: line 42, column 5 - mapping values are      │ │  │ │
│  │  │ Validates against the OpenAPI 3.0 JSON Schema        │ │  │ │
│  │  │   Ready for the next validation layer                │ │  │ │
content.caption: Three-step validation ensures OpenAPI specifications are technically correct
Running Specification Validation
content.code:
# Using swagger-cli (most common)
npx swagger-cli validate openapi.yaml

# Example output when valid:
# ✅ openapi.yaml is valid

# Example output when invalid:
# ❌ Error: #/paths/~1users/post
#   Property 'post' is not expected to exist here.
#   Did you mean 'post'? (typo: should be 'post' not 'post')

# Using openapi-spec-validator (Python)
pip install openapi-spec-validator
openapi-spec-validator openapi.yaml

# Using vacuum (Go, very fast)
vacuum lint openapi.yaml

# Validate and bundle external references into one file
npx swagger-cli bundle openapi.yaml --outfile bundled.yaml --type yaml

content.caption: Common Specification Errors and Fixes
content.code:
# ERROR 1: Missing required field
# ❌ This fails validation
openapi: 3.0.3
paths: {}
# Missing 'info' section!

# ✅ Fixed version
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: My API
  version: 1.0.0
paths: {}

# ERROR 2: Invalid HTTP method
# ❌ This fails (typo in method name)
paths:
  /users:
    gett:  # Should be 'get'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK

# ✅ Fixed version
paths:
  /users:
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK

# ERROR 3: Broken $ref
# ❌ This fails (User schema doesn't exist)
components:
  schemas:
    User:
      type: object
      properties:
        name:
          type: string

paths:
  /users:
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Usr'  # Typo!

# ✅ Fixed version
# Change to '#/components/schemas/User'

content.value: Once your spec is valid, the next question is: is it well-written? Does it follow API design best practices? Are descriptions clear? Are operation IDs consistent? This is where linting tools like Spectral come in. They enforce your API style guide automatically, catching issues that would otherwise be caught only in code review—or worse, not caught at all.

content.title: Spectral Linting Flow
content: │  │  │ For each rule, traverse spec with JSONPath              │ │ │
│  │  │         → Add: description: Returns a list of users     │ │ │
│  │  │         → Add: description: The user's unique ID        │ │ │
content.caption: Spectral applies rules to enforce API style and best practices
Custom Spectral Ruleset
content.code:
# .spectral.yaml
# A comprehensive ruleset for API style enforcement

# Extend the built-in OpenAPI ruleset
extends: [["spectral:oas", "all"]]

# Override severity of built-in rules
rules:
  oas3-valid-schema-example: warn
  operation-description: error
  parameter-description: error

# Custom rules
  operation-id-kebab-case:
    description: Operation IDs must be kebab-case
    severity: error
    given: $.paths[*][get,post,put,patch,delete]
    then:
      field: operationId
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        match: '^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$'

  require-response-description:
    description: All responses must have descriptions
    severity: error
    given: $.paths.*.*.responses.*
    then:
      field: description
      function: truthy

  no-empty-description:
    description: Descriptions cannot be empty strings
    severity: error
    given: $..description
    then:
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        notMatch: '^\s*$'

  require-examples:
    description: Complex schemas should have examples
    severity: warn
    given: $.components.schemas.*
    where:
      - field: type
        matches: object
    then:
      field: example
      function: truthy

  snake-case-in-path:
    description: Path segments should be snake_case
    severity: warn
    given: $.paths[*]~
    then:
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        match: '^\/([a-z0-9_]+(?:\/[a-z0-9_]+)*)?$'

  no-eval-in-description:
    description: Descriptions shouldn't contain 'eval'
    severity: warn
    given: $..description
    then:
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        notMatch: '\beval\b'

content.caption: Running Spectral in CI
content.code:
# Lint with custom rules
npx spectral lint -r .spectral.yaml openapi.yaml

# Output JSON for further processing
npx spectral lint -f json openapi.yaml > lint-results.json

# Fail only on errors (allow warnings)
npx spectral lint --fail-severity=error openapi.yaml

# GitHub Action example
# .github/workflows/lint-openapi.yml
name: Lint OpenAPI
on: pull_request

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      - run: npm install -g @stoplight/spectral-cli
      - name: Lint OpenAPI
        run: |
          spectral lint -r .spectral.yaml openapi.yaml
          if [ $? -eq 1 ]; then
            echo "❌ OpenAPI has errors"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "✅ OpenAPI passed linting"

content.value: This layer catches contract violations at runtime. Every time your API receives a request or sends a response, you can validate it against the OpenAPI spec. This is especially valuable during development and testing—it immediately tells you when your implementation doesn't match your contract.

content.title: Runtime Validation Flow
content: │  │  │ 1. Find matching path and operation in spec             │ │ │
│  │  API IMPLEMENTATION (ONLY IF REQUEST IS VALID)              │ │
content.caption: Runtime validation catches contract violations before they reach clients
Python Request/Response Validation
content.code:
from openapi_core import create_spec
from openapi_core.validation.request.validators import RequestValidator
from openapi_core.validation.response.validators import ResponseValidator
import requests
import yaml

class APIContractValidator:
    def __init__(self, spec_path):
        with open(spec_path) as f:
            spec_dict = yaml.safe_load(f)
            self.spec = create_spec(spec_dict)
        self.request_validator = RequestValidator(self.spec)
        self.response_validator = ResponseValidator(self.spec)
    
    def validate_request(self, method, path, body=None, headers=None):
        """Validate a request against the spec"""
        # Create request object
        class Request:
            method = method
            path = path
            body = body or b''
            headers = headers or {}
            mimetype = headers.get('Content-Type', 'application/json')
        
        result = self.request_validator.validate(Request())
        if result.errors:
            for error in result.errors:
                print(f"❌ Request validation failed: {error}")
            return False
        return True
    
    def validate_response(self, request, response):
        """Validate a response against the spec"""
        result = self.response_validator.validate(request, response)
        if result.errors:
            for error in result.errors:
                print(f"❌ Response validation failed: {error}")
            return False
        return True

# Usage in tests
validator = APIContractValidator('openapi.yaml')

# Test a request
response = requests.post(
    'https://api.example.com/users',
    json={'name': 'John', 'email': 'john@e.com'}
)

# Validate the response
if not validator.validate_response(response.request, response):
    raise Exception('Contract violation!')

content.caption: Express Middleware for Validation

content.value: Runtime validation catches mistakes in individual calls, but contract testing goes further: it automatically tests every documented endpoint against a live API, ensuring that the entire contract is honored. Dredd is the most popular tool for this, and it's like having an automated QA engineer that never sleeps.

content.title: Dredd Testing Architecture
content: │  │  │   - Create request from examples or generate data       │ │ │
│  │  │   - Note expected response code and body                 │ │ │
│  │  │ STEP 3: SEND REQUESTS TO LIVE API                       │ │ │
content.caption: Dredd tests ensure your running API matches the OpenAPI specification
Dredd Hooks for Test Setup
Dredd Configuration
content.code:
# dredd.yml
# Configuration file for Dredd

# Where your OpenAPI spec is
openapi: ./openapi.yaml

# Your API endpoint
endpoint: http://localhost:3000

# Language for hooks (JavaScript)
language: nodejs

# Hook files to run
hookfiles: ./hooks/*.js

# Request headers to add to all requests
headers:
  X-API-Version: v2
  Accept: application/json
  User-Agent: dredd/1.0

# Output reporters
reporter: 
  - dot
  - html
  - junit

# Output files
output:
  - ./reports/dredd.html
  - ./reports/dredd.xml

# Color output
color: true

# Log level
loglevel: warning

# Timeout for each request in milliseconds
timeout: 30000

# Number of concurrent requests
concurrency: 10

# Use examples from spec for test data
data:
  useExamples: true

# Skip some paths (useful for WIP endpoints)

content.value: The most expensive kind of API bug is one that breaks existing clients. Once clients are in production, you cannot change your API in ways that would break them without going through a deprecation process. Breaking change detection tools analyze two versions of your OpenAPI spec and tell you exactly what changed and whether those changes are backward compatible.

content.title: Breaking vs Non-breaking Changes
content: │  │  │   • Parameter 'page' changed from optional to required│ │  │
│  │  │   • New optional field 'phone' added to response    │ │  │
content.caption: Automated diffing helps identify which changes require a major version bump
Running OpenAPI Diff
content.code:
# Using oas-diff (Node.js)
npx oas-diff openapi-v1.yaml openapi-v2.yaml

# Output:
# 🔴 Breaking changes:
#   - DELETE /users/{id} endpoint removed
#     This will break clients that delete users
#   - Parameter 'page' now required (was optional)
#     Existing clients not sending page will fail
#   - Response field 'user.email' removed
#     Clients expecting email will crash
# 
# 🟢 Non-breaking changes:
#   + POST /users/batch endpoint added
#   + New optional field 'user.phone' added
#   + New enum value 'premium' added to 'role'
# 
# ⚠️  Deprecations:
#   - GET /users/all deprecated (use /users with pagination)

# Using openapi-diff (Java)
java -jar openapi-diff.jar openapi-v1.yaml openapi-v2.yaml --markdown report.md

# Using oasdiff (Go)
oasdiff breaking openapi-v1.yaml openapi-v2.yaml --format json

# Generate changelog
oasdiff changelog openapi-v1.yaml openapi-v2.yaml

content.value:
OpenAPI validation transforms your API specification from a static document into an executable contract. By validating at multiple levels—from the spec itself to individual requests and responses to complete contract testing—you build a comprehensive quality system that catches issues at every stage of development.

The tools and techniques covered in this guide form a complete validation stack:

- **Specification validation** ensures your OpenAPI document is well-formed
- **Linting** enforces style consistency and best practices
- **Runtime validation** catches contract violations during development
- **Contract testing** verifies all endpoints work as documented
- **Breaking change detection** protects existing clients from unexpected changes

Implementing this stack requires effort, but the payoff is enormous: fewer production incidents, happier API consumers, and the confidence to evolve your API without fear of breaking things. Your OpenAPI spec becomes not just documentation, but a powerful tool for quality assurance.

tutorials.title: API Blueprint & RAML Documentation
tutorials.description: API Blueprint syntax, RAML specifications, and tools for documentation validation and testing.

content.value:
Before OpenAPI became the universal standard, there were other players in the API description space. API Blueprint and RAML both emerged around 2013-2014 as powerful alternatives to Swagger (which later became OpenAPI). While OpenAPI has won the format war, you'll still encounter these specifications in legacy systems, and they offer some unique approaches that are worth understanding.

API Blueprint takes a documentation-first approach—it's designed to be readable by humans first and machines second. RAML (RESTful API Modeling Language) takes a design-first approach—it emphasizes reusability and modularity through inheritance and traits. Both have their own ecosystems of tools and are still used in production by many organizations.

content.title: API Description Language Timeline
content: │               └── RAML and API Blueprint usage declines         │
content.caption: OpenAPI has emerged as the dominant standard for API description

content.value: API Blueprint is a documentation-oriented API description language. It's written in Markdown with a specific syntax, making it incredibly readable for humans while still being machine-parsable. The philosophy is simple: your API documentation should be written for humans first, and if it can be parsed by machines too, that's a bonus.

content.caption: Basic API Blueprint Example
content.code:
FORMAT: 1A

# Polls API

Simple API for creating and managing polls.

# Group Polls
Resources related to polls in the API.

## Polls Collection [/polls]

### List All Polls [GET]

Returns a list of all polls.

+ Response 200 (application/json)
    + Body

            [
                {
                    "id": 1,
                    "question": "Favorite programming language?",
                    "created_at": "2025-01-15T10:00:00Z"
                },
                {
                    "id": 2,
                    "question": "Best API format?",
                    "created_at": "2025-01-16T14:30:00Z"
                }
            ]

### Create a New Poll [POST]

Creates a new poll.

+ Request (application/json)
    + Body

            {
                "question": "Your favorite color?",
                "options": ["Red", "Green", "Blue"]
            }

+ Response 201 (application/json)
    + Body

            {
                "id": 3,
                "question": "Your favorite color?",
                "created_at": "2025-01-17T09:15:00Z"
            }

## Poll [/polls/{id}]

### Retrieve a Poll [GET]

Returns a single poll by ID.

+ Parameters
    + id: 1 (number) - Poll ID

+ Response 200 (application/json)
    + Body

            {
                "id": 1,
                "question": "Favorite programming language?",
                "created_at": "2025-01-15T10:00:00Z",
                "options": [
                    {
                        "id": 101,
                        "text": "Python",
                        "votes": 42
                    },
                    {
                        "id": 102,
                        "text": "JavaScript",
                        "votes": 38
                    }
                ]
            }

+ Response 404 (application/json)
    + Body

            {
                "error": "Poll not found"
            }

### Delete a Poll [DELETE]

Deletes an existing poll.

+ Parameters
    + id: 1 (number) - Poll ID

+ Response 204

content.title: API Blueprint Syntax Deep Dive
content.explanation:
**FORMAT: 1A**
The first line must specify the API Blueprint version. 1A is the most common version.

**# Headers**
`#` for API name, `##` for resource group, `###` for individual resources, `####` for actions.

**Resource Groups**
`# Group <name>` organizes related resources.

**Resources and URIs**
`## Resource Name [/path/{param}]` defines a resource with optional URI parameters.

**Actions**
`### Action Name [METHOD]` defines an HTTP method.

**Parameters**
`+ Parameters` section lists URI parameters with type, example, and description.

**Requests and Responses**
`+ Request (content-type)` describes a request with optional body.
`+ Response <status-code> (content-type)` describes a response.

**Headers**
`+ Headers` section can specify custom headers.

**Attributes**
`+ Attributes` defines expected structure (similar to JSON Schema).

content.caption: Advanced API Blueprint with Attributes
content.code:
FORMAT: 1A

# Advanced Polls API

## Data Structures

### Poll (object)
+ id: 1 (number) - Poll identifier
+ question: Favorite color? (string) - Poll question
+ created_at: 2025-01-17T09:15:00Z (string) - Creation timestamp
+ options (array[Option])

### Option (object)
+ id: 101 (number) - Option identifier
+ text: Python (string) - Option text
+ votes: 42 (number) - Vote count

### NewPoll (object)
+ question: Your favorite color? (string, required)
+ options: Red, Green, Blue (array[string], required)

# Group Polls

## Polls Collection [/polls]

### List All Polls [GET]

+ Response 200 (application/json)
    + Attributes (array[Poll])

### Create a New Poll [POST]

+ Request (application/json)
    + Attributes (NewPoll)

+ Response 201 (application/json)
    + Attributes (Poll)

+ Response 400 (application/json)
    + Attributes (object)
        + error: Validation failed (string)
        + details (array[object])
            + field: question (string)
            + message: Question is required (string)

## Poll [/polls/{id}]

### Retrieve a Poll [GET]

+ Parameters
    + id: 1 (number) - Poll ID

+ Response 200 (application/json)
    + Attributes (Poll)

+ Response 404 (application/json)
    + Attributes (object)
        + error: Poll not found (string)

### Update a Poll [PATCH]

+ Parameters
    + id: 1 (number) - Poll ID

+ Request (application/json)
    + Attributes (object)
        + question: Updated question? (string, optional)

+ Response 200 (application/json)
    + Attributes (Poll)

### Delete a Poll [DELETE]

+ Parameters
    + id: 1 (number) - Poll ID

+ Response 204

content.value: RAML (RESTful API Modeling Language) takes a different approach from API Blueprint. It's designed for reusability and modularity, with features like inheritance, traits, and resource types. RAML is YAML-based, making it familiar to anyone who's used to configuration files. Its design-first philosophy means you can design your API completely before writing any code.

content.caption: Basic RAML Example
content.code:
#%RAML 1.0
title: Polls API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}
mediaType: application/json

types:
  Poll:
    type: object
    properties:
      id: number
      question: string
      createdAt: datetime
    example:
      id: 1
      question: Favorite programming language?
      createdAt: 2025-01-15T10:00:00Z
  
  NewPoll:
    type: object
    properties:
      question:
        type: string
        required: true
      options:
        type: array
        items: string
        required: true
    example:
      question: Your favorite color?
      options: [Red, Green, Blue]
  
  Error:
    type: object
    properties:
      error: string
      code: number

traits:
  pageable:
    queryParameters:
      page:
        description: Page number
        type: integer
        required: false
        default: 1
      limit:
        description: Items per page
        type: integer
        required: false
        default: 20
        maximum: 100
  secured:
    headers:
      Authorization:
        description: Bearer token
        type: string
        required: true
        pattern: ^Bearer .+$

resourceTypes:
  collection:
    get:
      description: List all <<resourcePathName>>
      responses:
        200:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: <<type>>[]
    post:
      description: Create a new <<resourcePathName|!singularize>>
      body:
        application/json:
          type: <<postType>>
      responses:
        201:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: <<type>>
  
  member:
    get:
      description: Get a <<resourcePathName|!singularize>> by ID
      responses:
        200:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: <<type>>
        404:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: Error
    delete:
      description: Delete a <<resourcePathName|!singularize>>
      responses:
        204:

/polls:
  type:
    collection:
      type: Poll
      postType: NewPoll
  get:
    is: [pageable, secured]
  /{id}:
    type:
      member:
        type: Poll
    get:
      description: Retrieve a specific poll with its options
      responses:
        200:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: Poll
              properties:
                options:
                  type: array
                  items:
                    properties:
                      id: number
                      text: string
                      votes: number
    /options:
      post:
        description: Add an option to a poll
        body:
          application/json:
            properties:
              text: string
        responses:
          201:
            body:
              application/json:
                properties:
                  id: number
                  text: string

content.title: RAML Core Concepts
content.explanation:
**Types** define reusable data structures. RAML supports JSON Schema-like definitions with examples.

**Traits** are reusable sets of query parameters, headers, or responses that can be applied to multiple methods. Common traits include pagination, sorting, filtering, and authentication.

**Resource Types** are templates for common resource patterns. The example shows a collection pattern (GET list + POST create) and a member pattern (GET, PUT, DELETE).

**Libraries** allow splitting large APIs into multiple files.

**Overlays** and **Extensions** allow modifying existing API definitions for different environments or versions.

**Annotations** add custom metadata to any element.

content.caption: RAML with Libraries and Overlays
content.code:
# main.raml
#%RAML 1.0
title: Enterprise API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}

uses:
  common: libraries/common.raml
  security: libraries/security.raml
  errors: libraries/errors.raml

/users:
  get:
    is: [common.pageable, common.sortable, security.token]
    responses:
      200:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: common.User[]
      429:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: errors.RateLimitError

# libraries/common.raml
#%RAML 1.0 Library
types:
  User:
    properties:
      id: string
      email: string
      name: string

traits:
  pageable:
    queryParameters:
      page:
        type: integer
        default: 1
      limit:
        type: integer
        default: 20
  sortable:
    queryParameters:
      sortBy:
        type: string
        required: false
      sortOrder:
        enum: [asc, desc]
        default: asc

# overlays/production.raml
#%RAML 1.0 Overlay
usage: Production-specific settings
masterRef: main.raml

baseUri: https://prod-api.example.com/v1

/users:
  get:
    is: [security.rateLimit: { limit: 1000 }]

content.value: If you're maintaining a legacy API with API Blueprint or RAML, you might need to migrate to OpenAPI for better tooling and ecosystem support. Here are practical migration strategies.

content.title: Migration Paths
content.caption: Migration tools provide a starting point, but manual review is essential for quality
API Blueprint to OpenAPI
content.code:
# Install conversion tool
npm install -g api-blueprint-to-swagger

# Convert
api-blueprint-to-swagger api.apib > openapi.yaml

# Alternatively, use apib2swagger
npm install -g apib2swagger
apib2swagger -i api.apib -o openapi.json

# Validate the result
npx swagger-cli validate openapi.yaml

# Fix common issues
# 1. Add missing info section if not present
# 2. Convert MSON attributes to JSON Schema
# 3. Add examples where conversion lost them

content.caption: RAML to OpenAPI
content.code:
# Install conversion tool
npm install -g raml2swagger

# Convert
raml2swagger api.raml > openapi.yaml

# Alternative: Use OAS RAML Converter (Java)
java -jar oas-raml-converter.jar -from raml -to oas20 api.raml openapi.json

# For RAML 1.0 to OpenAPI 3.0
npx @mulesoft/raml-to-oas api.raml -o openapi.yaml

# Validate
npx swagger-cli validate openapi.yaml

# Common issues to fix:
# 1. Traits may need manual conversion
# 2. Resource types may need expansion
# 3. Libraries need to be bundled first

# Bundle libraries first
raml-validator --bundle api.raml > bundled.raml
raml2swagger bundled.raml > openapi.yaml

content.value:
While OpenAPI has become the dominant standard, understanding API Blueprint and RAML is valuable for maintaining legacy systems and appreciating the evolution of API description languages.

API Blueprint's human-first approach makes it excellent for documentation-focused teams. RAML's design-first philosophy with traits and resource types offers powerful reusability that some teams still prefer.

If you're starting a new project today, OpenAPI is the clear choice. But if you're working with existing systems using these specifications, the tools and techniques in this guide will help you keep them reliable while planning a gradual migration to OpenAPI.

tutorials.title: Complete API Governance & Standards
tutorials.description: Naming conventions, versioning policies, security standards, compliance requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS), and API lifecycle management.

content.value:
API governance is the practice of establishing and enforcing standards across your API ecosystem. It's the difference between a chaotic collection of independently designed APIs and a cohesive platform that developers love to use. Without governance, you end up with inconsistent naming, incompatible versioning strategies, security holes, and compliance violations.

Think of governance like urban planning. Without it, you get a chaotic sprawl where buildings are placed haphazardly, streets don't connect, and infrastructure fails. With governance, you get a well-designed city where everything works together. APIs are the buildings of the digital city—governance ensures they form a coherent, usable, and safe environment.

content.title: API Governance Pyramid
content.caption: API governance builds from design principles up through compliance requirements

content.value: Effective governance doesn't mean bureaucracy. It means creating standards that make APIs easier to build, use, and maintain. When done right, governance accelerates development by providing clear patterns and preventing common mistakes. It's a force multiplier, not a bottleneck.

Consistent naming is the foundation of API usability. When every endpoint follows predictable patterns, developers can guess how your API works without looking at documentation. This section establishes naming standards for resources, parameters, and operations.

content.title: Naming Convention Standards
rows: Plural indicates collection, hyphens improve readability

content.caption: Good vs Bad Naming Examples
OpenAPI Example with Naming Standards
content.code:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: E-commerce API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /products:
    get:
      summary: List products
      parameters:
        - name: page
          in: query
          schema:
            type: integer
            default: 1
        - name: pageSize
          in: query
          schema:
            type: integer
            default: 20
        - name: sortBy
          in: query
          schema:
            type: string
            enum: [name, price, createdAt]
        - name: sortOrder
          in: query
          schema:
            type: string
            enum: [ASC, DESC]
            default: ASC
  /products/{productId}:
    get:
      summary: Get product by ID
      parameters:
        - name: productId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
            pattern: '^[a-z0-9-]+$'
components:
  schemas:
    Product:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
          example: "prod-123"
        name:

content.code:
# rate_limiter.py
import time
from collections import defaultdict
import redis

class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, redis_client=None):
        self.redis = redis_client or redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0)
    
    def check_rate_limit(self, key, limit=1000, window=3600):
        """
        Check if request is within rate limit
        Returns (allowed, remaining, reset_time)
        """
        now = int(time.time())
        window_start = now - window
        
        # Use Redis sorted set for sliding window
        pipeline = self.redis.pipeline()
        pipeline.zremrangebyscore(key, 0, window_start)
        pipeline.zcard(key)
        pipeline.zadd(key, {now: now})
        pipeline.expire(key, window)
        results = pipeline.execute()
        
        request_count = results[1]
        
        if request_count > limit:
            # Get oldest request in window to calculate reset
            oldest = self.redis.zrange(key, 0, 0, withscores=True)
            reset_time = int(oldest[0][1]) + window if oldest else now + window
            return False, 0, reset_time
        
        remaining = limit - request_count
        return True, remaining, now + window
    
    def get_headers(self, key, limit=1000):
        allowed, remaining, reset = self.check_rate_limit(key, limit)
        return {
            'X-RateLimit-Limit': str(limit),
            'X-RateLimit-Remaining': str(remaining),
            'X-RateLimit-Reset': str(reset)
        }

# Usage in Flask
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)
rate_limiter = RateLimiter()

@app.before_request
def check_rate_limit():
    # Rate limit by API key or IP
    api_key = request.headers.get('X-API-Key')
    key = api_key or request.remote_addr
    
    allowed, remaining, reset = rate_limiter.check_rate_limit(f"ratelimit:{key}")
    
    # Add headers to response
    request.rate_limit_headers = {
        'X-RateLimit-Limit': '1000',
        'X-RateLimit-Remaining': str(remaining),
        'X-RateLimit-Reset': str(reset)
    }
    
    if not allowed:
        return jsonify({
            'error': 'RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED',
            'message': 'Rate limit exceeded',
            'reset': reset
        }), 429

@app.after_request
def add_rate_limit_headers(response):
    if hasattr(request, 'rate_limit_headers'):
        response.headers.update(request.rate_limit_headers)
    return response

from flask import Blueprint, request, jsonify
import json
from datetime import datetime

gdpr_bp = Blueprint('gdpr', __name__, url_prefix='/api/v1')

@GDPR_bp.route('/users/<user_id>/personal-data', methods=['GET'])
def get_personal_data(user_id):
    """GDPR Right to Access - return all personal data"""
    user = find_user(user_id)
    if not user:
        return jsonify({'error': 'USER_NOT_FOUND'}), 404
    
    # Collect all personal data across systems
    personal_data = {
        'user': user.to_dict(),
        'profile': get_user_profile(user_id),
        'preferences': get_user_preferences(user_id),
        'activity': get_user_activity(user_id),
        'communications': get_user_communications(user_id)
    }
    
    # Log the access for audit
    log_data_access({
        'user_id': user_id,
        'accessed_by': request.headers.get('X-User-ID'),
        'timestamp': datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        'reason': 'GDPR access request'
    })
    
    return jsonify(personal_data)

@GDPR_bp.route('/users/<user_id>/personal-data', methods=['DELETE'])
def delete_personal_data(user_id):
    """GDPR Right to Erasure - delete all personal data"""
    # Verify identity (strong authentication required)
    if not verify_identity(user_id, request):
        return jsonify({'error': 'UNAUTHORIZED'}), 401
    
    # Delete data across all systems
    tasks = [
        delete_user(user_id),
        delete_profile(user_id),
        delete_preferences(user_id),
        anonymize_activity(user_id)
    ]
    
    # Wait for all deletions to complete

    # Log deletion for audit

# .spectral.yaml
# Comprehensive governance ruleset

extends: [["spectral:oas", "all"]]

rules:
  # Naming conventions
  operation-id-kebab-case:
    description: Operation IDs must be kebab-case
    severity: error
    given: $.paths[*][get,post,put,patch,delete]
    then:
      field: operationId
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        match: '^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$'
  
  camel-case-parameters:
    description: Query parameters must be camelCase
    severity: error
    given: $.paths.*.*.parameters[?(@.in=='query')]
    then:
      field: name
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        match: '^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$'
  
  # Documentation requirements
  require-description:
    description: All operations must have descriptions
    severity: error
    given: $.paths[*][get,post,put,patch,delete]
    then:
      field: description
      function: truthy
  
  require-examples:
    description: Complex schemas should have examples
    severity: warn
    given: $.components.schemas.*
    where:
      - field: type
        matches: object
    then:
      field: example
      function: truthy
  
  # Security requirements
  require-https:
    description: APIs must use HTTPS
    severity: error
    given: $.servers[*].url
    then:
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        match: '^https://'
  
  require-auth:
    description: APIs must define authentication
    severity: error
    given: $
    then:
      field: components.securitySchemes
      function: truthy
  
  require-rate-limiting:
    description: Rate limiting headers should be documented
    severity: warn
    given: $.paths.*.*.responses.*.headers
    then:
      field: X-RateLimit-Limit
      function: truthy
  
  # Versioning requirements
  version-format:
    description: Version must follow semantic versioning
    severity: error
    given: $.info.version
    then:
      function: pattern
      functionOptions:
        match: '^v?\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-[a-zA-Z0-9.]+)?$'
  
  # Compliance rules
  gdpr-data-access-endpoint:
    description: APIs handling personal data must have GDPR access endpoint

content.value:
API governance is not about bureaucracy—it's about consistency, security, and quality. When implemented well, governance accelerates development by providing clear patterns and preventing common mistakes.

Start with a small set of essential standards: naming conventions, versioning policy, security requirements, and error formats. Automate what you can with Spectral and CI/CD pipelines. Establish clear ownership and review processes. Then gradually expand as your API ecosystem grows.

The result is an API platform that developers love to use—predictable, secure, and well-documented. Your consumers will thank you, your security team will thank you, and your future self will thank you when you need to maintain or evolve these APIs.

content.value:
When money is involved, testing becomes critical. A bug in rate limiting can cost you revenue. A mistake in quota enforcement can overcharge customers. An error in usage analytics can lead to billing disputes. API monetization testing ensures that your business logic works as intended and that your customers are billed correctly for what they use.

Think of monetization testing as auditing your cash register. You wouldn't run a store without checking that the register calculates correctly, that prices are right, and that customers aren't overcharged. The same applies to APIs that generate revenue.

content.value: Rate limiting protects your API from abuse and enforces tier-based access. Testing rate limits ensures that legitimate users aren't blocked and that abusers are stopped at the right thresholds.

content.title: Rate Limiting Algorithms
content.explanation:
**Token Bucket**: Tokens added at fixed rate, requests consume tokens. Allows bursts.
**Leaky Bucket**: Requests processed at fixed rate, queues excess. Smooths traffic.
**Fixed Window**: Count requests in fixed time window (e.g., per minute). Simple but can allow spikes at boundaries.
**Sliding Window**: More accurate, counts requests in rolling window. Prevents boundary spikes.

**Test each algorithm for:**
- Burst behavior
- Window boundaries
- Concurrent requests
- Distributed consistency

content.code:
import pytest
import requests
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

class TestRateLimiting:
    BASE_URL = "https://api.example.com/v1"
    API_KEY = "test-key-123"
    
    def test_rate_limit_headers(self):
        """Verify rate limit headers are present and correct"""
        response = requests.get(
            f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
            headers={"X-API-Key": self.API_KEY}
        )
        
        assert response.status_code == 200
        assert 'X-RateLimit-Limit' in response.headers
        assert 'X-RateLimit-Remaining' in response.headers
        assert 'X-RateLimit-Reset' in response.headers
        
        limit = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Limit'])
        remaining = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Remaining'])
        reset = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Reset'])
        
        assert limit == 1000  # Default tier limit
        assert remaining == 999  # One request used
        assert reset > time.time()  # Reset time in future
    
    def test_rate_limit_enforcement(self):
        """Test that hitting the limit returns 429"""
        limit = 10  # Test with small limit
        
        # Consume all requests up to limit
        for i in range(limit):
            response = requests.get(
                f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
                headers={"X-API-Key": self.API_KEY}
            )
            assert response.status_code == 200
            remaining = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Remaining'])
            assert remaining == limit - i - 1
        
        # Next request should be rate limited
        response = requests.get(
            f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
            headers={"X-API-Key": self.API_KEY}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 429
        data = response.json()
        assert data['code'] == 'RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED'
        assert 'retry-after' in data
        
        # Check retry-after header
        retry_after = int(response.headers.get('Retry-After', 0))
        assert retry_after > 0
    
    def test_rate_limit_reset(self):
        """Test that limits reset after the window"""
        # Get current reset time
        response = requests.get(
            f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
            headers={"X-API-Key": self.API_KEY}
        )
        reset_time = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Reset'])
        
        # Wait for reset
        wait_time = max(0, reset_time - time.time() + 1)
        time.sleep(wait_time)
        
        # Should have full quota again
        response = requests.get(
            f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
            headers={"X-API-Key": self.API_KEY}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 200
        remaining = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Remaining'])
        limit = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Limit'])
        assert remaining == limit - 1  # Used one request
    
    def test_burst_behavior(self):
        """Test token bucket burst allowance"""
        # Send requests in rapid succession
        def send_request():
            return requests.get(
                f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
                headers={"X-API-Key": self.API_KEY}
            )
        
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=20) as executor:
            futures = [executor.submit(send_request) for _ in range(50)]
            responses = [f.result() for f in futures]
        
        # Count successes and failures
        successes = sum(1 for r in responses if r.status_code == 200)
        failures = sum(1 for r in responses if r.status_code == 429)
        
        # Should allow burst up to limit
        assert successes == 10  # Assuming limit is 10
        assert failures == 40
    
    def test_different_tiers(self):
        """Test rate limits for different subscription tiers"""
        tiers = {
            'free': {'key': 'free-key', 'limit': 10},
            'pro': {'key': 'pro-key', 'limit': 100},
            'enterprise': {'key': 'enterprise-key', 'limit': 1000}
        }
        
        for tier, config in tiers.items():
            # Make one request to get headers
            response = requests.get(
                f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
                headers={"X-API-Key": config['key']}
            )
            assert response.status_code == 200
            
            limit = int(response.headers['X-RateLimit-Limit'])
            assert limit == config['limit'], f"{tier} tier limit mismatch"
    
    def test_concurrent_rate_limiting(self):
        """Test rate limiting under concurrent load"""
        import threading
        import queue
        
        results = queue.Queue()
        
        def worker():
            for _ in range(5):
                response = requests.get(
                    f"{self.BASE_URL}/test",
                    headers={"X-API-Key": self.API_KEY}
                )
                results.put(response.status_code)
        
        # Start 10 concurrent workers
        threads = []
        for _ in range(10):
            t = threading.Thread(target=worker)
            t.start()
            threads.append(t)
        
        for t in threads:
            t.join()
        
        # Collect results
        statuses = []
        while not results.empty():
            statuses.append(results.get())
        
        successes = statuses.count(200)
        failures = statuses.count(429)
        
        # Total requests: 10 workers * 5 requests = 50
        # Limit is 10, so should have 10 successes, 40 failures
        assert successes == 10
        assert failures == 40

class TestQuotaEnforcement:
    def test_monthly_quota(self):
        """Test monthly quota enforcement"""
        api_key = "test-monthly-key"
        monthly_limit = 100
        
        # Consume almost all quota
        for i in range(monthly_limit - 1):
            response = requests.get(
                f"{BASE_URL}/test",

            )
            assert response.status_code == 200
            
            # Check remaining quota in headers
            remaining = int(response.headers.get('X-Quota-Remaining', 0))
            assert remaining == monthly_limit - i - 1
        
        # Last allowed request
        response = requests.get(
            f"{BASE_URL}/test",
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 200
        
        # Next request should exceed quota
        response = requests.get(

            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 403  # Forbidden (quota exceeded)
        data = response.json()
        assert data['code'] == 'QUOTA_EXCEEDED'
        
        # Should have upgrade options
        assert 'upgrade_url' in data
    
    def test_quota_reset(self):
        """Test that quota resets at billing cycle"""
        api_key = "test-reset-key"
        
        # Get current quota info

            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        reset_time = int(response.headers.get('X-Quota-Reset', 0))
        
        # Wait for reset
        wait_time = max(0, reset_time - time.time() + 1)
        if wait_time > 0:
            time.sleep(wait_time)
        
        # Quota should be restored
        response = requests.get(
            f"{BASE_URL}/test",
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 200
        
        # Check headers show full quota
        limit = int(response.headers.get('X-Quota-Limit', 0))
        remaining = int(response.headers.get('X-Quota-Remaining', 0))
        assert remaining == limit - 1  # One request used
    
    def test_quota_upgrade_mid_cycle(self):
        """Test upgrading tier mid-billing cycle"""
        api_key = "test-upgrade-key"
        
        # Use some quota at free tier
        for _ in range(5):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Get current usage
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage_before = response.json()['current_usage']
        
        # Upgrade to pro tier
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/subscription/upgrade",
            json={"tier": "pro"},
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 200
        
        # Check new quota
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        limit = int(response.headers.get('X-Quota-Limit', 0))
        remaining = int(response.headers.get('X-Quota-Remaining', 0))
        
        # Should have pro tier quota (e.g., 1000)
        assert limit == 1000
        # Should have used some quota already
        assert remaining == limit - usage_before - 1
    
    def test_quota_downgrade(self):
        """Test downgrading and overage handling"""
        api_key = "test-downgrade-key"
        
        # Use more than free tier allows
        for _ in range(50):  # Free tier might be 10
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Try to downgrade to free
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/subscription/downgrade",
            json={"tier": "free"},
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        
        # Should be rejected or warn about overage
        assert response.status_code == 409  # Conflict
        data = response.json()
        assert 'overage' in data
        assert data['current_usage'] > data['new_tier_limit']
        
        # Should offer options
        assert 'reduce_usage' in data or 'pay_for_overage' in data
    
    def test_quota_notifications(self):
        """Test quota threshold notifications"""
        api_key = "test-notify-key"
        
        # Set up webhook listener for testing
        notifications = []
        
        def webhook_handler(request):
            notifications.append(request.json)
            return "OK", 200
        
        # Use quota to trigger notifications
        # At 80%, 90%, 100% thresholds
        for i in range(100):
            response = requests.get(
                f"{BASE_URL}/test",
                headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
            )
            
            # Check if notification was sent
            if i == 79:  # 80% threshold
                time.sleep(1)  # Give time for async notification
                assert any(n['threshold'] == 80 for n in notifications)
            elif i == 89:  # 90% threshold

class TestUsageTracking:
    def test_request_counting_accuracy(self):
        """Test that every request is counted accurately"""
        api_key = "test-count-key"
        num_requests = 100
        
        # Reset usage (test-only endpoint)
        requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/test/reset-usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Make requests
        for _ in range(num_requests):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Check reported usage
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage = response.json()
        
        assert usage['total_requests'] == num_requests
        assert usage['successful_requests'] == num_requests
        assert usage['failed_requests'] == 0
    
    def test_failed_requests_tracking(self):
        """Test that failed requests are tracked separately"""
        api_key = "test-fail-key"
        
        # Make requests to invalid endpoint
        for _ in range(5):
            response = requests.get(
                f"{BASE_URL}/invalid",
                headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
            )
            assert response.status_code == 404
        
        # Check usage
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage = response.json()
        
        assert usage['failed_requests'] == 5
        
        # Make successful requests
        for _ in range(3):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Check again
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage = response.json()
        
        assert usage['successful_requests'] == 3
        assert usage['failed_requests'] == 5  # Failed still counted
    
    def test_no_double_counting_on_retries(self):
        """Test that retries don't double-count usage"""
        api_key = "test-retry-key"
        
        # Configure client with retries
        session = requests.Session()
        adapter = requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter(max_retries=3)
        session.mount('https://', adapter)
        
        # Reset usage
        requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/test/reset-usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Make request that triggers retry (e.g., 503 then success)
        # This requires a test endpoint that fails first then succeeds
        response = session.get(
            f"{BASE_URL}/test/unstable",
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 200
        
        # Check usage - should be 1, not 4 (original + 3 retries)
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage = response.json()
        assert usage['total_requests'] == 1
    
    def test_batch_request_counting(self):
        """Test that batch requests count each operation"""
        api_key = "test-batch-key"
        
        # Reset usage
        requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/test/reset-usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Send batch request with 10 operations
        batch = []
        for i in range(10):
            batch.append({
                'method': 'GET',
                'path': '/test',
                'id': f'req-{i}'
            })
        
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/batch",
            json=batch,
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 200
        
        # Check usage - should be 10, not 1
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage = response.json()
        assert usage['total_requests'] == 10
    
    def test_streaming_message_counting(self):
        """Test that streaming counts each message"""
        api_key = "test-stream-key"
        
        # Reset usage
        requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/test/reset-usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Establish streaming connection
        import websocket
        ws = websocket.WebSocket()
        ws.connect(f"wss://api.example.com/stream?api_key={api_key}")
        
        # Send 50 messages
        for i in range(50):
            ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "ping", "seq": i}))
        
        ws.close()
        
        # Check usage
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage = response.json()
        
        # Should count each message, not the connection
        assert usage['stream_messages'] == 50
        assert usage['stream_connections'] == 1
    
    def test_usage_consistency_across_systems(self):
        """Test that usage counts are consistent across systems"""
        api_key = "test-consistency-key"
        
        # Make some requests
        for _ in range(25):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Get usage from different sources
        usage_api = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}).json()
        usage_raw = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/admin/usage/{api_key}", headers={"X-Admin-Key": "admin"}).json()
        usage_db = query_database(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM usage WHERE api_key = '{api_key}'")
        
        # All should match
        assert usage_api['total_requests'] == usage_raw['total'] == usage_db
    
    def test_real_time_usage_updates(self):
        """Test that usage updates are near real-time"""
        api_key = "test-realtime-key"
        
        # Make request
        start = time.time()
        requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Check usage immediately
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/usage/current", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        usage = response.json()
        
        # Should see the request within seconds
        assert usage['current_minute'] >= 1
        assert time.time() - start < 5  # Within 5 seconds

class TestBillingAccuracy:
    def test_pay_as_you_go_billing(self):
        """Test pay-as-you-go pricing model"""
        api_key = "test-payg-key"
        price_per_request = 0.001  # $0.001 per request
        
        # Make 1000 requests
        for _ in range(1000):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Generate invoice
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/billing/generate-invoice",
            json={"api_key": api_key, "period": "current"}
        )
        invoice = response.json()
        
        expected_charge = 1000 * price_per_request
        assert invoice['total'] == expected_charge
        assert invoice['items'][0]['quantity'] == 1000
        assert invoice['items'][0]['unit_price'] == price_per_request
    
    def test_tiered_pricing(self):
        """Test tiered pricing (e.g., first 1000 free, then $0.001)"""
        api_key = "test-tiered-key"
        
        # Make 2500 requests
        for _ in range(2500):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Generate invoice
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/billing/generate-invoice",
            json={"api_key": api_key, "period": "current"}
        )
        invoice = response.json()
        
        # First 1000 free, next 1500 at $0.001
        expected_charge = 1500 * 0.001
        assert invoice['total'] == expected_charge
        
        # Should have tier breakdown
        tiers = invoice['tiers']
        assert tiers[0]['range'] == "0-1000"
        assert tiers[0]['charge'] == 0
        assert tiers[1]['range'] == "1001-2500"
        assert tiers[1]['charge'] == expected_charge
    
    def test_monthly_subscription(self):
        """Test fixed monthly subscription"""
        api_key = "test-sub-key"
        monthly_price = 99.00
        
        # Make many requests (should be covered by subscription)
        for _ in range(10000):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Generate invoice
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/billing/generate-invoice",
            json={"api_key": api_key, "period": "current"}
        )
        invoice = response.json()
        
        # Should be flat monthly fee
        assert invoice['total'] == monthly_price
        assert len(invoice['items']) == 1
        assert invoice['items'][0]['description'] == "Monthly subscription"
    
    def test_hybrid_pricing(self):
        """Test subscription + overage pricing"""
        api_key = "test-hybrid-key"
        monthly_price = 49.00
        included_requests = 5000
        overage_price = 0.0005
        
        # Make 7500 requests (2500 overage)
        for _ in range(7500):
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Generate invoice
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/billing/generate-invoice",
            json={"api_key": api_key, "period": "current"}
        )
        invoice = response.json()
        
        expected_charge = monthly_price + (2500 * overage_price)
        assert invoice['total'] == expected_charge
        assert len(invoice['items']) == 2
    
    def test_prorated_upgrades(self):
        """Test prorated charges when upgrading mid-cycle"""
        api_key = "test-prorate-key"
        
        # Start with basic tier at beginning of month
        requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/subscription/change",
            json={"tier": "basic"},
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        
        # Halfway through month, upgrade to pro
        time.sleep(15 * 24 * 3600)  # 15 days later
        
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/subscription/upgrade",
            json={"tier": "pro"},
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        upgrade_data = response.json()
        
        # Should have prorated charge
        assert 'prorated_charge' in upgrade_data
        assert upgrade_data['prorated_charge'] > 0
        
        # End of month invoice should include both
        invoice = generate_invoice(api_key)
        
        # Basic tier for first half, pro for second half
        assert invoice['total'] == upgrade_data['prorated_charge'] + (49.00 * 0.5)
    
    def test_credits_and_discounts(self):
        """Test applying credits and discounts"""
        api_key = "test-credit-key"
        
        # Add $50 credit
        requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/billing/add-credit",
            json={"amount": 50.00},
            headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}
        )
        
        # Generate $30 in usage
        for _ in range(30000):  # $0.001 each = $30
            requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/test", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key})
        
        # Invoice should be $0, credit should be reduced
        invoice = generate_invoice(api_key)
        assert invoice['total'] == 0
        
        # Check remaining credit
        credit = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/billing/credit", headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}).json()

        # Generate another $30 usage

        # Invoice should be $10 (used remaining $20 credit)

    def test_billing_boundaries(self):

        # Make requests exactly at month boundary
        # This requires controlling the system clock or using a test endpoint
        
        # Request at 23:59:59
